2. HCRs and MSEs: an introduction

Grant Adams

Source: vignettes/hcrs-and-mses.Rmd
hcrs-and-mses.Rmd

This vignette fits an operating model and a Tier 3 estimation model, runs a management strategy evaluation with run_mse(), then compares alternative reference points, survey frequencies, assessment schedules and a climate-linked operating model.

Fitting the operating model

A management strategy evaluation (MSE; Punt et al. 2016) runs a management strategy in closed loop: an operating model (OM) represents the “true” stock and generates data, an estimation model (EM) is fitted to that data and applies a harvest control rule (HCR), and the resulting catch feeds back into the OM. This example uses the Gulf of Alaska northern rockfish assessment as the OM.

library(Rceattle)
data("NorthernRockfish2022")
nrdata <- NorthernRockfish2022
nrdata$fleet_control$Proj_F_proportion <- 1

om <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list = nrdata,
  estimateMode = 0,  # Estimate
  initMode = 1,      # Assume unfished equilibrium
  M1Fun = build_M1(
    M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",
    linkages = list(
      M1 = linkage_spec(
        formula = ~ 1,
        priors = list(
          "(Intercept)" = lognormal(log(0.06), 0.05)
        )
      )
    )
  ),
  fit_control = fit_control(phase = TRUE)
)

Fitting the estimation model (Tier 3 HCR)

fit_mod(HCR = build_hcr()) sets the harvest control rule and its reference points. Here the EM uses the NPFMC Tier 3 rule: fishing at F40%, the maxFABC rate, with an F35% overfishing limit (FOFL, the Amendment-56 SPR proxy for FMSY). Below the B40% target, F ramps down linearly, reaching zero when SSB falls to Alpha = 0.05 of that target. Plimit = 0.2 is a separate shutoff: fishing stops when the stock is assessed below 20% of unfished SSB. See ?build_hcr for the available rules and reference points.

em <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list = nrdata,
  estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
  initMode = 1,      # Assume unfished equilibrium
  M1Fun = build_M1(
    M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",
    linkages = list(
      M1 = linkage_spec(
        formula = ~ 1,
        priors = list(
          "(Intercept)" = lognormal(log(0.06), 0.05)
        )
      )
    )
  ),
  HCR = build_hcr(HCR = "NPFMC", # Tier3 HCR
                  Ftarget = 0.4, # F40%
                  Flimit = 0.35, # F35%
                  Plimit = 0.2,  # No fishing when SB<SB20
                  Alpha = 0.05),
  fit_control = fit_control(verbose = 1, phase = TRUE)
)

Running the MSE

run_mse() projects the OM, samples data every sampling_period years, re-fits the EM every assessment_period years, and applies the EM’s HCR to the OM. nsim sets the number of stochastic trajectories.

Parameters you fixed in the EM’s map that Rceattle would otherwise estimate stay fixed at each re-fit, and run_mse() reports how many; see ?run_mse for years after the EM’s endyr and what does not carry forward.

Check endyr before you start

The OM and the EM must share a terminal year and a projection horizon; mismatched years are refused.

Every year after endyr is a projection year whose catch the control rule sets, so catch recorded past endyr is blanked to NA at setup and run_mse() warns and names the years. That warning almost always means endyr has fallen behind the data, which the likelihood scores only for Year <= endyr. To condition the assessment on those years, move endyr up and refit both models; leave it, and the MSE simulates those years instead.

mse1 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em,
  nsim = 10,
  assessment_period = 2,
  # BTS = fleet 1 (biennial), Fishery = fleet 2 (annual)
  sampling_period = c(2, 1),
  seed = 666 # default; per-sim seed = seed + sim
)

Reproducibility

  • seed (default 666) sets the draws inside each simulated trajectory (recruitment, observation error, composition resampling): simulation sim calls set.seed(seed + sim), so simulation 1 uses seed 667. The same call with the same seed reproduces the trajectories bit-for-bit, with no set.seed() needed beforehand.
  • regenerate_seed (defaults to seed) sets the one observation-error draw in the optional regenerate_past = TRUE step, shared by every simulation; under simulate_data = FALSE that step uses the OM’s expected values.

Reproducibility holds within a package version, not across one:

  • 5.9.0 and 5.18.0 move the random-number stream for every seeded run_mse(simulate_data = TRUE), so a seeded run from before either does not reproduce after it; 5.9.0 also moves a seeded self_test().
  • 5.13.0 is a boundary only for a run using a scalar cap, or one whose control rule reads reference points from an estimated stock-recruit curve.
  • 5.70.4 changes a seeded run_mse(regenerate_past = TRUE, simulate_data = TRUE).

simulate_data = FALSE is unaffected by 5.9.0 and 5.18.0. The stream position is data-dependent, so changing an unrelated covariance or composition sample size moves everything drawn after it. sim_mod() redraws stomach contents only where suitability is estimated; run_mse() always keeps the observed ones.

For management-facing runs, save packageVersion("Rceattle") and the seed with the .rds.

Evaluating the MSE with plots

The OM’s SSB depletion across simulations shows the range of stock trajectories the strategy produces.

plot_ssb_depletion(lapply(mse1, function(x) x$OM))
plot_ssb_depletion(
  c(mse1$Sim_1$EM,           # EMs
    list(mse1$Sim_1$OM,      # OM
         mse1$Sim_1$OM_no_F  # OM with no fishing after the original OM's endyr
    )),    
  line_col = c(
    paste0("grey", round(seq(80, 50, length.out = 15))),
    1, 3
  )
)

Summary statistics

mse_summary() reduces the trajectories to performance statistics. It returns a list: $species (one row per species), $fleet (one row per fishery fleet), $total (a named vector across the whole system), and $meta (the number of simulations, species and fishery fleets, and the harvest control rule).

mse_summ <- mse_summary(mse1)
names(mse_summ)

knitr::kable(mse_summ$species, digits = 2)
knitr::kable(mse_summ$fleet, digits = 2)

In the metric columns (avg_catch, catch_iav, om_p_overfishing, em_p_overfished, …), om_ is what the operating model did and em_ what the estimation model believed; p_overfishing_false_pos and its siblings are where the two disagree.

Alternative scenarios

The runs below vary the reference points, the survey frequency, the assessment interval with sampling effort, and the environment (mse5 is mse4 with a climate-linked OM), for comparison against mse1.

Different reference points

Here the EM uses a more aggressive rule: an F30% target, an F10% limit, and Plimit = 0, so there is no SB0-based shutoff; F still reaches zero below Alpha = 0.1 of B30%.

em2 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list = nrdata,
  estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
  initMode = 1,      # Assume unfished equilibrium
  M1Fun = build_M1(
    M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",
    linkages = list(
      M1 = linkage_spec(
        formula = ~ 1,
        priors = list(
          "(Intercept)" = lognormal(log(0.06), 0.05)
        )
      )
    )
  ),
  HCR = build_hcr(HCR = "NPFMC", # Tier3 HCR
                  Ftarget = 0.30,# F30%
                  Flimit = 0.10, # F10%
                  Plimit = 0,    # No limit
                  Alpha = 0.1),
  fit_control = fit_control(verbose = 1, phase = TRUE)
)

mse2 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em2, 
  nsim = 10, 
  assessment_period = 2,
  sampling_period = c(2, 1) # BTS = fleet 1, Fishery = fleet 2
)

Triennial bottom-trawl survey

sampling_period = c(3, 1) samples the bottom-trawl survey (BTS, fleet 1) only every third year and the fishery (fleet 2) every year.

mse3 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em, 
  nsim = 10, 
  assessment_period = 2,
  sampling_period = c(3, 1) # BTS = fleet 1, Fishery = fleet 2
)

4-year assessment cycle and reduced survey coverage

The EM is re-fitted only every fourth year (assessment_period = 4), and fut_sample = 0.5 halves future sampling effort on both data streams: composition sample sizes are halved and the index log-SD is doubled (Log_sd * 1 / fut_sample).

mse4 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em, 
  nsim = 10, 
  fut_sample = 0.5,
  assessment_period = 4,
  sampling_period = c(2, 1) # BTS = fleet 1, Fishery = fleet 2
)

A missed assessment, and a buffer while advice is stale

The scenarios above set a period. For one skipped assessment in an otherwise regular cycle, assessment_period also takes the schedule itself, as a vector of the years an assessment is completed. A period is a permanent policy whose cost compounds; one missed assessment is a single episode of stale advice, whose cost depends on the stock’s state when the gap opens.

biennial <- seq(om$data_list$endyr + 2, om$data_list$projyr, by = 2)
miss_yr  <- biennial[ceiling(length(biennial) / 3)]

mse6 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em,
  nsim = 10,
  assessment_period = setdiff(biennial, miss_yr), # every year but miss_yr
  sampling_period = c(2, 1)
)

To pair the gap with a precautionary reduction, give catch_mult a data.frame of Year, Species (the species number) and mult; any pair the table omits is multiplied by 1.

The assessment in year Y sets catch for Y+1 onward, so a missed assessment leaves the two years after it on the previous assessment’s advice, not the missed year itself, which the previous assessment sets in the baseline too.

schedule <- setdiff(biennial, miss_yr)

# The years the missed assessment would have set: from the year after it,
# through the next assessment that was completed.
gap_yrs <- (miss_yr + 1):min(schedule[schedule > miss_yr])

# 10% reduction, held for exactly those years.
buffer <- expand.grid(Year = gap_yrs, Species = seq_len(om$data_list$nspp))
buffer$mult <- 0.90

mse7 <- run_mse(
  om = om, em = em,
  nsim = 10,
  assessment_period = schedule,
  sampling_period = c(2, 1),
  catch_mult = buffer
)

Compare these with a baseline that differs only in the schedule (same om, em and seed), as paired within-replicate differences. Schedules on the same seed share their recruitment deviations, and each assessment’s observation draws are seeded on that assessment’s own year, so an assessment in year Y starts from the same place in every schedule that assesses Y.

Common random numbers are not complete, though. One sim_mod() call draws every year in the assessment interval under that assessment’s seed, so two schedules that differ in which years they assess realize different observation error in the years between, even where the stock is in the same state. The paired difference is therefore mostly, but not entirely, the schedule; size the replicate count accordingly. Once two schedules genuinely diverge (different catch taken, different years surveyed), their draws diverge too, which is a real difference between the runs, not noise.

Make the last assessment year reach the projection horizon. Catch is filled only up to the last assessment year, so a schedule that stops short leaves the trailing years at NA, and mse_summary() summarises over the whole projection, so it understates average catch, catch IAV and P(Closed); run_mse() warns when this happens. A biennial cycle over an odd number of projection years always does this: seq(2027, 2050, by = 2) ends at 2049 against a 2050 horizon.

catch_mult multiplies catch, not ABC. A real ABC reduction changes removals only to the extent the fishery attains ABC, so either scale the multiplier by recent attainment, 1 - (1 - mult) * attainment, or report the unscaled result as an upper bound on the effect of the reduction.

Climate-linked MSE

Here OM recruitment (via R0) tracks a steadily rising environmental covariate, so the OM’s productivity shifts over time while the EM keeps assuming stationary recruitment.

Climate-linked OM 


# Generate random env data
projyrs <- nrdata$styr:nrdata$projyr
projnyrs <- length(projyrs)

# Env data
# Build the table over styr:projyr so the trend runs into the projection;
# years past the last row would take a zero offset.
nrdata$env_data <- data.frame(Year = projyrs,
                              EnvIndex = seq(0, 1, length.out = projnyrs))

# Fit OM
om2 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list = nrdata,
  estimateMode = 0,  # Estimate
  initMode = 1,      # Assume unfished equilibrium
  M1Fun = build_M1(
    M1_model = "sex_age_invariant",
    linkages = list(
      M1 = linkage_spec(
        formula = ~ 1,
        priors = list(
          "(Intercept)" = lognormal(log(0.06), 0.05)
        )
      )
    )
  ),
  recFun = build_srr(
    srr_fun = "mean",    # Mean R with covariates
    proj_mean_rec = FALSE,
    linkages = list(
      R0 = linkage_spec(formula = ~ EnvIndex)
    )),
  fit_control = fit_control(phase = TRUE)
)

plot_biomass(om2, incl_proj = TRUE)

Run MSE 

mse5 <- run_mse(
  om = om2, em = em, 
  nsim = 10, 
  fut_sample = 0.5,
  assessment_period = 4,
  sampling_period = c(2, 1) # BTS = fleet 1, Fishery = fleet 2
)

Overall summary

To put the strategies side by side, label one entity of each summary (here $species) and stack those, not the whole list.

stack_species <- function(x, label) {
  out <- x$species
  out$MSE <- label
  out
}

knitr::kable(
  rbind(stack_species(mse_summary(mse1), 1),
        stack_species(mse_summary(mse2), 2)) |>
    dplyr::relocate(MSE),
  digits = 2)

References

  • Punt, A.E., Butterworth, D.S., de Moor, C.L., De Oliveira, J.A.A., Haddon, M. (2016). Management strategy evaluation: best practices. Fish and Fisheries, 17, 303-334.
